architectural_implications.after: A model abstraction boundary plus a per-candidate evaluation suite that acts as a merge gate for model and prompt changes.
architectural_implications.before: A single hard-coded model with a hand-tuned prompt; correctness assumed to be a property of the prompt.
architectural_implications.consequence: Model upgrades become PRs with scorecards; the eval set and test corpus become the most valuable and most maintained asset in the repo.
architectural_implications.observation: Model choice is currently implicit in application code (model name + prompt text).

architectural_implications.after: A validation and sanitization layer at the execution boundary that rejects unexpected or invented arguments before side effects occur.
architectural_implications.before: JSON schema is declared in the tool definition and schema conformance is trusted.
architectural_implications.consequence: Argument-level hallucination becomes a caught, observable error rather than a silent bad write, and swap-induced behavior changes surface as validation failures.
architectural_implications.observation: Tool arguments generated by the model are passed toward side-effecting APIs.

architectural_implications.after: Prompts as build artifacts compiled per model, with the optimizer config and eval set in version control and a known-good fallback prompt for degraded mode.
architectural_implications.before: One canonical prompt string shipped with the app.
architectural_implications.consequence: Swap cost moves from manual re-prompting to a recompile-and-verify pipeline; prompt text alone no longer describes system behavior.
architectural_implications.observation: Prompt optimization produces model-specific prompts from a metric and dataset.

article_ideas.angle: Contrast the prompt-instruction assumption against the workshop's observed behavior and derive the eval dimension and guardrail placement that follows.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers building production RAG pipelines and platform teams owning model selection
article_ideas.based_on: Abstention under incomplete retrieval context is a model-level capability
article_ideas.thesis: Grounding failures in RAG are a model-level capability gap, not a prompt-engineering gap: adding 'only answer from context' does not stop weaker models from substituting parametric knowledge, so faithfulness must be enforced by model selection plus an external guardrail and measured as a separate abstention dimension in every swap gate.
article_ideas.title: Your RAG Prompt Cannot Save a Model That Won't Abstain

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the trust boundary: move trust from the tool schema in the prompt to runtime enforcement before side effects, and treat swap-induced argument changes as caught validation failures rather than silent bad writes.
article_ideas.audience: Agent platform engineers and security-minded backend architects
article_ideas.based_on: Treat tool arguments as untrusted input
article_ideas.thesis: The dangerous failure in agent tool calling is not wrong-tool selection but invented arguments, and since schema declaration does not guarantee schema-conformant generation, agent runtimes must validate and sanitize model-produced arguments at the execution boundary exactly as they would treat external user input.
article_ideas.title: Tool Arguments Are Untrusted Input

article_ideas.angle: Use the availability framing to argue that prompt tuning budget should be redirected into regression harnesses, with turn count, abstention rate, and argument-error rate as scorecard rows.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders and platform teams responsible for vendor portability
article_ideas.based_on: Model swapping is framed as an availability/portability requirement
article_ideas.thesis: Because model swapping is driven by provider availability rather than cost tuning, the model is a swappable dependency; changing the model name is equivalent to a dependency upgrade and must ship as a PR with a per-candidate scorecard, making the eval set and test corpus the most valuable maintained asset in the repository.
article_ideas.title: Model Swaps Are Dependency Upgrades, So Gate Them Like One

article_ideas.angle: Apply the model-swap logic reflexively to the grader, and recommend mixing deterministic string checks with judged checks to bound judge-induced error.
article_ideas.audience: Eval and quality engineers, applied research teams
article_ideas.based_on: The judge is itself a model
article_ideas.thesis: LLM-as-a-judge makes the evaluation stack inherit the same swap-sensitivity as the system under test, so an uncalibrated judge can manufacture or mask regressions; eval infrastructure must be versioned, rubric-explicit, and periodically re-validated against human labels before any swap delta is trusted.
article_ideas.title: The Judge Is Also Being Swapped

connections.relationship: Model portability is only safe when a regression harness validates each candidate model; the eval set is what makes the abstraction boundary usable.

connections.connects_to: untrusted input validation at the execution boundary
connections.relationship: Model-generated arguments should be treated with the same skepticism as external user input, moving trust from schema declaration to runtime enforcement.

connections.connects_to: agent loop turn and cost budgets
connections.relationship: Per-model parallelization ability determines loop depth, so max-turn limits and cost budgets must be derived from measured model efficiency.
Optimization converts prompt text into a model-specific build output generated from a metric and dataset, changing how prompts are versioned and swapped.
The grader is itself a swappable model, so judge choice and calibration become part of the evaluation's own validity surface.

evidence_quotes.text: AI engineers need options to switch models dynamically if access to a specific model is cut off or performance varies.

core_insights.generalization: Any system whose core capability is supplied by an external, single-vendor model should be designed with a substitution path and a validation gate, mirroring how teams treat database or cloud-provider portability.
core_insights.insight: Model swapping is framed as an availability/portability requirement — the ability to route around a cut-off or degraded model provider — rather than a cost-optimization nicety, which makes the model a swappable dependency that must be validated like any other dependency upgrade.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If model identity is treated as a runtime configuration rather than a compile-time assumption, the engineering budget shifts from prompt tuning to regression harnesses that gate each swap.

evidence_quotes.text: Smaller models are more likely to ignore context constraints and hallucinate information from their weights.
Models like GPT-5.5 are better at explicitly stating when information is missing from the provided context.
When provided with context that lacks answers to a user query, smaller models frequently invent answers based on internal weights rather than citing missing data.

core_insights.generalization: Faithfulness constraints should be treated as a per-model measured property, with abstention rate as a first-class benchmark dimension separate from answer quality.
core_insights.insight: Abstention under incomplete retrieval context is a model-level capability, not a prompt-level instruction: when the retrieved context does not contain the answer, smaller models fall back to parametric knowledge and fabricate, while stronger models explicitly report the gap.
core_insights.why_it_matters: RAG grounding failures therefore cannot be fixed by adding 'only answer from context' to the prompt; the guardrail must live outside the model or the model choice must be constrained by a grounding-specific eval.

evidence_quotes.text: Models differ in argument correctness and hallucinating unexpected arguments (e.g., adding self as an attendee).
All frontier agents rely on tool calling as their fundamental building block.

core_insights.generalization: Treat tool arguments as untrusted input: validate, constrain, and reject at the execution boundary, since schema-conformant generation is not guaranteed by schema declaration.
core_insights.insight: Tool-call failure is not primarily about selecting the wrong tool but about argument-level hallucination — models inventing plausible-but-unrequested fields (e.g., inserting themselves as an attendee) — which requires schema validation and argument sanitization outside the model rather than trust in schema conformance.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Agent runtimes that forward model-generated arguments directly into side-effecting APIs inherit correctness and security risk from a per-model behavior that varies silently across swaps.

evidence_quotes.text: Models vary in efficiency, with some achieving goals in a single parallel turn and others requiring multiple sequential tool calls.

core_insights.generalization: Agent runtimes should measure turns-to-completion and parallel-call ratio as model-specific performance characteristics alongside accuracy, and set budgets from data rather than fixed defaults.
core_insights.insight: Parallel tool-calling competence changes agent loop structure, not just latency: some models reach the goal in a single parallel turn while others require multiple sequential tool calls, producing large variance in turn count, cost, and intermediate state exposure under an identical prompt.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Loop designs, budgets, and max-turn limits calibrated against one model will silently under- or over-provision when the model is swapped; turn count becomes a measurable per-model efficiency metric.

evidence_quotes.text: DSPy allows developers to declare program specs and constraints rather than manually tweaking prompt text.
Prompt optimization automates finding prompts that satisfy complex constraints across models.

core_insights.generalization: Where output constraints are complex and model-conditional, declarative program specs plus an optimizer scale better than manual prompt iteration, at the cost of losing a single prompt that works everywhere.
core_insights.insight: Automated prompt optimization inverts prompt portability: instead of a hand-written prompt that travels across models, prompts become compiled artifacts generated per model against a metric and test set, so a model swap becomes a recompilation rather than a drop-in replacement.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This reframes prompt engineering as a build step with a compiler, a dataset, and a metric — which means the eval set and optimizer configuration are production assets, and unoptimized fallback prompts become a degraded-mode requirement.

evidence_quotes.text: LLM-as-a-judge requires calibration against human input and robust grading rubrics.
Running evals is time-intensive and costly, requiring well-curated test cases to prevent model drift.

core_insights.generalization: Evaluation infrastructure should be versioned and periodically re-validated against human ground truth, exactly like the system it evaluates.
core_insights.insight: The judge is itself a model: LLM-as-a-judge grading requires calibration against human labels and explicit rubrics, so the evaluation stack has the same swap-sensitivity problem as the system under test.
core_insights.why_it_matters: An uncalibrated judge can mask or manufacture regressions during a model swap; teams need a validated judge (or a mix of deterministic string checks plus judged checks) before trusting eval deltas.

evidence_quotes.text: Language switching (e.g., prompting in Spanish) can cause models to hallucinate or fail tasks.

core_insights.generalization: Eval suites should stratify by incidental input properties (language, encoding format, image quality) that are orthogonal to the task but known to shift model behavior.
core_insights.insight: Input language is a reliability variable, not merely an i18n concern: prompting in a non-English language (e.g., Spanish) can cause a model that otherwise succeeds to hallucinate or fail the same multimodal task.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Multilingual applications can regress on a model swap even when English-language evals are green, meaning test stratification must include input language as a dimension.

evidence_quotes.text: Models differ in argument correctness and hallucinating unexpected arguments (e.g., adding self as an attendee).
All frontier agents rely on tool calling as their fundamental building block.

project_ideas.based_on: invented plausible-but-unrequested fields (e.g., inserting themselves as an attendee)
project_ideas.hypothesis: Strict argument validation and sanitization at the execution boundary reduces side-effecting bad writes from model-generated tool arguments to zero while preserving task success rate, and argument-error rate varies measurably across models under an identical tool schema.
project_ideas.measurement: Bad writes reaching the sink per model (target: zero with validator), rejection rate per model, and task success rate delta between validator-on and validator-off arms.
project_ideas.name: Argument Sentinel
project_ideas.poc: A fixed tool-calling harness with one side-effecting tool (e.g., booking with an attendee list). Run identical prompts across the workshop's candidate models with and without a validator that rejects unexpected/extra fields and enum violations before execution. Log every rejection.

project_ideas.based_on: When provided with context that lacks answers to a user query, smaller models frequently invent answers based on internal weights rather than citing missing data.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Injecting context-incomplete queries with known-missing answers into a RAG suite produces an abstention rate that separates models more sharply than answer-quality scores, and that rate is not improvable by prompt instruction alone on weaker models.
project_ideas.measurement: Fabrication rate on context-missing queries per model per arm, and drop in fabrication rate attributable to prompt instruction versus external check.
project_ideas.name: Abstention Gate
project_ideas.poc: A small RAG corpus with documented gaps (e.g., carpenter-bee documentation only). Query it with questions whose answers are absent. Compare three arms: baseline prompt, 'answer only from context' prompt, and an external abstention check that flags unsupported answers. Run across all candidate models.

project_ideas.based_on: Models vary in efficiency, with some achieving goals in a single parallel turn and others requiring multiple sequential tool calls.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Turns-to-completion and parallel-call ratio on an identical agent task differ enough across models that a fixed max-turn and cost budget calibrated on one model either truncates or over-provisions on another, and these metrics are stable enough within a version to set budgets from data.
project_ideas.measurement: Distribution of turns-to-completion, parallel-call ratio, token cost, and completed-vs-truncated rate at a fixed max-turn limit per model.
project_ideas.name: Turn Budget Profiler
project_ideas.poc: One multi-step tool task, one fixed harness, all four candidate models. Instrument turn count, parallel-call count, total tokens, and completion success. Repeat runs to estimate per-model variance and derive a budget per model.

project_ideas.based_on: How small can a stratified eval suite be while still catching grounding and tool-argument regressions
project_ideas.hypothesis: A stratified eval suite significantly smaller than a full benchmark can detect swap-induced grounding, tool-argument, and turn-efficiency regressions at a measurable detection rate, and detection rate per test case is highest for context-completeness and argument-shape stratification rather than task-type alone.
project_ideas.measurement: Regressions detected per suite size, detection rate per stratum, and cost per detected regression.
project_ideas.name: Swap Regression Detector
project_ideas.poc: Build a seeded regression corpus where each item has a known correct behavior. Simulate swaps across the candidate models, incrementally grow the suite by strata, and measure how many known swap-induced regressions are caught at each suite size.

source.author: AI Engineer
source.title: The Model Swap Workshop: GPT-5.5 vs Kimi vs DeepSeek vs Mistral — Pamela Fox, Microsoft

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Pamela Fox
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Comparing frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, and Mistral Large 3) across single-prompt calls, RAG, tool calling, agent loops, and evaluations.
  • Purpose: To demonstrate how frontier LLMs behave differently across common AI engineering tasks and to provide a reproducible workshop framework for evaluating and optimizing model swaps. Pamela Fox leads a hands-on workshop guiding AI engineers through model swapping across multiple frontier LLMs. Using Microsoft Foundry and Python, the workshop explores how models differ in reasoning, tool calling capacity, RAG grounding, multimodal image inputs, and agent loops. Attendees examine the practical trade-offs of switching models and evaluate them systematically using programmatic string comparisons, LLM-as-a-judge approaches, and assertion frameworks.

Topic Map

Workshop Setup and Introduction

  • Explanation: Introduction to the Model Swap Workshop, GitHub repository setup, environment variables, and model deployments in Microsoft Foundry.
  • Key claims:
    • AI engineers need options to switch models dynamically if access to a specific model is cut off or performance varies.
    • Environment variables in .env files manage API keys and model endpoints.
  • Examples:
    • Setting up GitHub Codespaces or cloning the repo locally using uv sync.
  • Terminology:
    • Microsoft Foundry
    • uv
    • GitHub Codespaces
    • .env
  • Why it matters: Establishes the infrastructure and motivation for model swapping in enterprise AI applications.

Single LLM Calls

  • Explanation: Running a simple letter counting prompt across different models to test reasoning and basic task execution.
  • Key claims:
    • Different models handle basic counting and multi-step reasoning tasks with varying accuracy.
    • Prompt engineering can bridge gaps between models.
  • Examples:
    • Counting occurrences of the letter 'e' in 'The elderly gentleman eagerly entered the elevator.'
  • Terminology:
    • GPT-5.5
    • Kimi K2.6
    • DeepSeek-V4-Flash
    • Mistral-Large-3
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that even basic tasks yield different results across models, highlighting the need for model evaluation.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

  • Explanation: Testing RAG pipelines to observe how models handle context grounding and refrain from hallucinating outside information.
  • Key claims:
    • Smaller models are more likely to ignore context constraints and hallucinate information from their weights.
    • Models like GPT-5.5 are better at explicitly stating when information is missing from the provided context.
  • Examples:
    • Asking about honey bee nest construction using a dataset that only contains carpenter bee documentation.
  • Terminology:
    • RAG
    • Grounding
    • Hallucination
    • Embeddings
  • Why it matters: Shows that model swap behavior heavily impacts factual accuracy and adherence to retrieved documents.

Multimodal Image Input

  • Explanation: Evaluating multimodal models on image understanding tasks, including object recognition and extracting data from small-font tables.
  • Key claims:
    • Multimodal models vary in their ability to process images and small-font tables.
    • Language switching (e.g., prompting in Spanish) can cause models to hallucinate or fail tasks.
  • Examples:
    • Classifying images of an ox vs. a unicorn and finding the cheapest plant in a table.
  • Terminology:
    • Multimodal
    • Base64 encoding
    • Image input
  • Why it matters: Crucial for applications processing mixed text and image inputs across different model providers.

Tool Calling (Function Calling)

  • Explanation: Exploring low-level tool calling using JSON schema definitions and evaluating whether models select correct tools and arguments.
  • Key claims:
    • All frontier agents rely on tool calling as their fundamental building block.
    • Models differ in argument correctness and hallucinating unexpected arguments (e.g., adding self as an attendee).
  • Examples:
    • Creating a calendar event from natural language user input using JSON schema definitions.
  • Terminology:
    • Tool calling
    • Function calling
    • JSON schema
    • Tool arguments
  • Why it matters: Tool calling forms the foundation of all modern AI agents and workflows.

Tool Calling in a Loop & Agent Frameworks

  • Explanation: Running multi-step tool calls in a loop and utilizing agent frameworks like LangChain and PydanticAI.
  • Key claims:
    • Models vary in efficiency, with some achieving goals in a single parallel turn and others requiring multiple sequential tool calls.
    • Agent frameworks provide abstraction over raw tool loops.
  • Examples:
    • Solving a multi-step word problem with a calculator tool and executing a travel planner agent.
  • Terminology:
    • Agent loop
    • LangChain
    • PydanticAI
    • Parallel tool calling
    • Turn
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates performance and cost implications of multi-turn agent interactions across models.

Evaluations (Evals)

  • Explanation: Building systematic evaluations using string comparisons, LLM-as-a-judge, and Microsoft Research's new 'ASSERT' framework.
  • Key claims:
    • Running evals is time-intensive and costly, requiring well-curated test cases to prevent model drift.
    • LLM-as-a-judge requires calibration against human input and robust grading rubrics.
  • Examples:
    • Evaluating travel planner model quality across dimensions like budget adherence and constraint satisfaction.
  • Terminology:
    • Evals
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • ASSERT
    • Stratification
    • Model drift
  • Why it matters: Essential for production readiness when swapping underlying LLM models.

Prompt Optimization

  • Explanation: Using DSPy and genetic algorithms (GEPA) to automatically optimize prompts against defined evaluation metrics and test sets.
  • Key claims:
    • Prompt optimization automates finding prompts that satisfy complex constraints across models.
    • DSPy allows developers to declare program specs and constraints rather than manually tweaking prompt text.
  • Examples:
    • Generating acrostic poems with strict word count and letter constraints using DSPy optimizers.
  • Terminology:
    • DSPy
    • GEPA
    • Genetic Pareto Algorithm
    • Prompt optimization
  • Why it matters: Reduces manual trial-and-error when adapting prompts to new models.

Key Points

Model Swapping Requires Systematic Evals

  • Explanation: Simply swapping model names in code without rigorous evaluation leads to silent failures and broken application workflows.
  • Evidence: Workshop comparisons showed different models failing at math, RAG grounding, and tool call sequencing under identical prompts.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must build comprehensive evaluation suites before deploying multi-model or swappable LLM architectures.

Smaller Models Hallucinate More in RAG Scenarios

  • Explanation: When provided with context that lacks answers to a user query, smaller models frequently invent answers based on internal weights rather than citing missing data.
  • Evidence: DeepSeek and Mistral models sometimes answered carpenter bee questions with honey bee details absent from context, whereas GPT-5.5 correctly stated no source was provided.
  • Practical implication: Strict prompt engineering and guardrails are necessary when using smaller or open-weight models for retrieval tasks.

Tool Calling Efficiency Varies Significantly

  • Explanation: Some models execute multi-step tool calls in parallel within a single turn, while others make multiple sequential calls, increasing latency and cost.
  • Evidence: GPT-5.5 completed calculator and travel planning tasks in fewer turns compared to other tested models.
  • Practical implication: Model choice directly impacts API cost and execution speed in agentic workflows.

Automated Prompt Optimization with DSPy

  • Explanation: Instead of manually tweaking prompts for different models, frameworks like DSPy use optimizers to automatically discover optimal prompts based on evaluation metrics.
  • Evidence: Using DSPy and GEPA to generate acrostic poem prompts that satisfy complex programmatic constraints.
  • Practical implication: Saves engineering time and improves model portability across different LLM backends.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

ASSERT Framework

  • How it works: Generates scenario-specific test cases and evaluation judges from a developer-defined spec, running models against target behaviors and scoring outputs across dimensions like budget adherence and constraint satisfaction.
  • Components:
    • Behavior categories
    • Test sets
    • Scenario generators
    • LLM-as-a-judge evaluation targets
  • When to use: When evaluating complex, multi-turn agent applications in production before model swaps.

DSPy (Declarative Self-improving Python)

  • How it works: Expresses tasks as structured signatures rather than raw prompts, using optimizers to automatically tune prompts and weights against programmatic constraints and metrics.
  • Components:
    • Signatures
    • Predictors
    • Metrics
    • Optimizers (GEPA)

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Pamela Fox
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Comparing frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, and Mistral Large 3) across single-prompt calls, RAG, tool calling, agent loops, and evaluations.
- **Purpose**: To demonstrate how frontier LLMs behave differently across common AI engineering tasks and to provide a reproducible workshop framework for evaluating and optimizing model swaps.
Pamela Fox leads a hands-on workshop guiding AI engineers through model swapping across multiple frontier LLMs. Using Microsoft Foundry and Python, the workshop explores how models differ in reasoning, tool calling capacity, RAG grounding, multimodal image inputs, and agent loops. Attendees examine the practical trade-offs of switching models and evaluate them systematically using programmatic string comparisons, LLM-as-a-judge approaches, and assertion frameworks.
## Topic Map
### Workshop Setup and Introduction
- **Explanation**: Introduction to the Model Swap Workshop, GitHub repository setup, environment variables, and model deployments in Microsoft Foundry.
- **Key claims**:
  - AI engineers need options to switch models dynamically if access to a specific model is cut off or performance varies.
  - Environment variables in .env files manage API keys and model endpoints.
- **Examples**:
  - Setting up GitHub Codespaces or cloning the repo locally using uv sync.
- **Terminology**:
  - Microsoft Foundry
  - uv
  - GitHub Codespaces
  - .env
- **Why it matters**: Establishes the infrastructure and motivation for model swapping in enterprise AI applications.
### Single LLM Calls
- **Explanation**: Running a simple letter counting prompt across different models to test reasoning and basic task execution.
- **Key claims**:
  - Different models handle basic counting and multi-step reasoning tasks with varying accuracy.
  - Prompt engineering can bridge gaps between models.
- **Examples**:
  - Counting occurrences of the letter 'e' in 'The elderly gentleman eagerly entered the elevator.'
- **Terminology**:
  - GPT-5.5
  - Kimi K2.6
  - DeepSeek-V4-Flash
  - Mistral-Large-3
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that even basic tasks yield different results across models, highlighting the need for model evaluation.
### Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
- **Explanation**: Testing RAG pipelines to observe how models handle context grounding and refrain from hallucinating outside information.
- **Key claims**:
  - Smaller models are more likely to ignore context constraints and hallucinate information from their weights.
  - Models like GPT-5.5 are better at explicitly stating when information is missing from the provided context.
- **Examples**:
  - Asking about honey bee nest construction using a dataset that only contains carpenter bee documentation.
- **Terminology**:
  - RAG
  - Grounding
  - Hallucination
  - Embeddings
- **Why it matters**: Shows that model swap behavior heavily impacts factual accuracy and adherence to retrieved documents.
### Multimodal Image Input
- **Explanation**: Evaluating multimodal models on image understanding tasks, including object recognition and extracting data from small-font tables.
- **Key claims**:
  - Multimodal models vary in their ability to process images and small-font tables.
  - Language switching (e.g., prompting in Spanish) can cause models to hallucinate or fail tasks.
- **Examples**:
  - Classifying images of an ox vs. a unicorn and finding the cheapest plant in a table.
- **Terminology**:
  - Multimodal
  - Base64 encoding
  - Image input
- **Why it matters**: Crucial for applications processing mixed text and image inputs across different model providers.
### Tool Calling (Function Calling)
- **Explanation**: Exploring low-level tool calling using JSON schema definitions and evaluating whether models select correct tools and arguments.
- **Key claims**:
  - All frontier agents rely on tool calling as their fundamental building block.
  - Models differ in argument correctness and hallucinating unexpected arguments (e.g., adding self as an attendee).
- **Examples**:
  - Creating a calendar event from natural language user input using JSON schema definitions.
- **Terminology**:
  - Tool calling
  - Function calling
  - JSON schema
  - Tool arguments
- **Why it matters**: Tool calling forms the foundation of all modern AI agents and workflows.
### Tool Calling in a Loop & Agent Frameworks
- **Explanation**: Running multi-step tool calls in a loop and utilizing agent frameworks like LangChain and PydanticAI.
- **Key claims**:
  - Models vary in efficiency, with some achieving goals in a single parallel turn and others requiring multiple sequential tool calls.
  - Agent frameworks provide abstraction over raw tool loops.
- **Examples**:
  - Solving a multi-step word problem with a calculator tool and executing a travel planner agent.
- **Terminology**:
  - Agent loop
  - LangChain
  - PydanticAI
  - Parallel tool calling
  - Turn
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates performance and cost implications of multi-turn agent interactions across models.
### Evaluations (Evals)
- **Explanation**: Building systematic evaluations using string comparisons, LLM-as-a-judge, and Microsoft Research's new 'ASSERT' framework.
- **Key claims**:
  - Running evals is time-intensive and costly, requiring well-curated test cases to prevent model drift.
  - LLM-as-a-judge requires calibration against human input and robust grading rubrics.
- **Examples**:
  - Evaluating travel planner model quality across dimensions like budget adherence and constraint satisfaction.
- **Terminology**:
  - Evals
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - ASSERT
  - Stratification
  - Model drift
- **Why it matters**: Essential for production readiness when swapping underlying LLM models.
### Prompt Optimization
- **Explanation**: Using DSPy and genetic algorithms (GEPA) to automatically optimize prompts against defined evaluation metrics and test sets.
- **Key claims**:
  - Prompt optimization automates finding prompts that satisfy complex constraints across models.
  - DSPy allows developers to declare program specs and constraints rather than manually tweaking prompt text.
- **Examples**:
  - Generating acrostic poems with strict word count and letter constraints using DSPy optimizers.
- **Terminology**:
  - DSPy
  - GEPA
  - Genetic Pareto Algorithm
  - Prompt optimization
- **Why it matters**: Reduces manual trial-and-error when adapting prompts to new models.
## Key Points
### Model Swapping Requires Systematic Evals
- **Explanation**: Simply swapping model names in code without rigorous evaluation leads to silent failures and broken application workflows.
- **Evidence**: Workshop comparisons showed different models failing at math, RAG grounding, and tool call sequencing under identical prompts.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must build comprehensive evaluation suites before deploying multi-model or swappable LLM architectures.
### Smaller Models Hallucinate More in RAG Scenarios
- **Explanation**: When provided with context that lacks answers to a user query, smaller models frequently invent answers based on internal weights rather than citing missing data.
- **Evidence**: DeepSeek and Mistral models sometimes answered carpenter bee questions with honey bee details absent from context, whereas GPT-5.5 correctly stated no source was provided.
- **Practical implication**: Strict prompt engineering and guardrails are necessary when using smaller or open-weight models for retrieval tasks.
### Tool Calling Efficiency Varies Significantly
- **Explanation**: Some models execute multi-step tool calls in parallel within a single turn, while others make multiple sequential calls, increasing latency and cost.
- **Evidence**: GPT-5.5 completed calculator and travel planning tasks in fewer turns compared to other tested models.
- **Practical implication**: Model choice directly impacts API cost and execution speed in agentic workflows.
### Automated Prompt Optimization with DSPy
- **Explanation**: Instead of manually tweaking prompts for different models, frameworks like DSPy use optimizers to automatically discover optimal prompts based on evaluation metrics.
- **Evidence**: Using DSPy and GEPA to generate acrostic poem prompts that satisfy complex programmatic constraints.
- **Practical implication**: Saves engineering time and improves model portability across different LLM backends.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### ASSERT Framework
- **How it works**: Generates scenario-specific test cases and evaluation judges from a developer-defined spec, running models against target behaviors and scoring outputs across dimensions like budget adherence and constraint satisfaction.
- **Components**:
  - Behavior categories
  - Test sets
  - Scenario generators
  - LLM-as-a-judge evaluation targets
- **When to use**: When evaluating complex, multi-turn agent applications in production before model swaps.
### DSPy (Declarative Self-improving Python)
- **How it works**: Expresses tasks as structured signatures rather than raw prompts, using optimizers to automatically tune prompts and weights against programmatic constraints and metrics.
- **Components**:
  - Signatures
  - Predictors
  - Metrics
  - Optimizers (GEPA)
- **When to use**: When building modular LLM applications that need to optimize prompts across different models automatically.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Testing DeepSeek-V4 Flash on letter counting ('How many times does the letter 'e' appear...?').
- **Illustrates**: Model reasoning limitations on specific structured extraction tasks.
- **Lesson**: Even advanced models fail simple character counting tasks without prompt guidance or reasoning steps.
### Mistral fabricated details from its weights despite system instructions not to hallucinate.
- **Illustrates**: Lack of grounding adherence in certain base models.
- **Lesson**: RAG applications require explicit negative constraints and robust eval judges.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Use the workshop GitHub repository (aka.ms/model-swap-code) to run examples locally or in GitHub Codespaces.
  - Employ 'uv' for fast Python package management and dependency syncing.
  - Implement programmatic evals (string comparison) for single tool calls before moving to LLM-as-a-judge.
- **Strategic**:
  - Never swap models in production without an evaluation suite quantifying quality, cost, and safety trade-offs.
  - Adopt automated prompt optimization (like DSPy) to achieve model independence and portability.
  - Design agents with parallel tool-calling capabilities in mind to optimize latency and cost.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do open-source models (via Ollama) compare to proprietary frontier models in agentic loops?
  - What is the optimal number of test cases required for reliable ASSERT evaluation suites?
  - How does prompt optimization overhead scale with complex multi-agent workflows?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- GPT-5.5 is available and deployed within Microsoft Foundry. (factual)
- ASSERT is a brand-new evaluation tool released by Microsoft Research. (factual)
- DSPy uses genetic algorithms (GEPA) for prompt optimization. (factual)
## Notable Quotes
> "Never just swap the model. I never just swapping the model. Prompt calculations, tool definitions, and output strategies all need tuning per model."
> "Evals can be a dry subject: data pipelines, metrics, LLM-as-a-judge calibration. But that doesn't mean we can't have fun with it."
> "LLMs are great at being coherent. You never have to check if an LLM is coherent."
